newsitem.title: USA: Lebed sacking unsettling for Russia, Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Lebed sacking unsettling for Russia, Clinton.

text.p: U.S. analysts believe the sacking of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed will not end the power struggles plaguing Russia.
They also say it could be bad news for President Bill Clinton, who hopes no major world crisis will erupt before the U.S. election on November 5.

Although authorised by the ailing President Boris Yeltsin, analysts said Lebed's dismissal was engineered by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other aides. Some analysts feared it could lead to renewed war in breakaway Chechnya.
Seeking to avoid inflaming Moscow's unstable political scene, U.S. officials kept public comment to a minimum.

They said it was an internal affair and Yeltsin acted "in accordance with his constitutional perogatives." The State Department said it was not '"a fundamental turning point" and that the Russian government was stable.

But privately there was deep concern. One analyst told Reuters Lebed's sacking could be "a nightmare" for the administration because further instability in Russia could provide Republican rivals with ammunition to attack Clinton.
More broadly, the looming election limits Clinton's ability to take action in the long-term U.S. interest without regard to domestic political consequences, this source said.
There remains a very real possibility that Lebed, Russia's most popular politician, could become president. The Americans expect him to remain a formidable force, even in opposition.
Yeltsin announced the sacking on Thursday on television, faulting Lebed for causing divisions in his governing team.
Earlier Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, an opponent of the peace deal Lebed negotiated in Chechnya, accused the former general of plotting to use force to seize power.

"This is all being portrayed as Yeltsin firing Lebed but this is essentially Chernomyrdin and other power ministers firing Lebed," said Charles King, a professor of government at Georgetown University. "Yeltsin signed the decree but he really wasn't in any shape to sign anything. He couldn't even put complete sentences together in Russian."
The Kremlin power struggle became increasingly intense and bitter after Yeltsin made public the severity of his illness on September 5 and said he would undergo heart surgery.

The operation is expected in November. Despite assurances, many experts believe Yeltsin's chances for a full recovery are less than 50 percent. With this uncertainty, even with Lebed out of government, "you'll see even more divisions among those (officials) who remain," King said in an interview.
American officials and private experts tended to dismiss allegations that Lebed was plotting some kind of a coup.
"I find such charges incredible," said Clifford Gaddy, an expert on the Russian economy with the Brookings Institution, a private think-tank.

He added: "Lebed has very much to lose (with a coup) and there is little chance of success in this. His real strength is among the population. He's the most popular political figure in Russia. Why would he risk that to become involved in some behind-the-scenes manipulation leading to a coup?"

Gaddy and other experts said they were puzzled by Lebed's recent alliance with Alexander Korzhakov, Yeltsin's former bodyguard and closest adviser who was dismissed several months ago. He was faulted for corruption and isolating Yeltsin.
Analysts believe this alliance was a factor in the dismissal of Lebed, whose strengths have been in opposing corruption and seeking to lower the crime rate.

Marshall Goldman of Harvard's Russian Research Centre said: "It's hard to explain Lebed's alliance with Korzhakov. Maybe he was looking for an ally against (Yeltsin chief of staff Anatoly) Chubais. But it has tainted Lebed's Mr. Clean image."
Many analysts are also concerned about the future of Lebed's August 31 peace deal with Chechen rebels, which hardliners in Moscow opposed.
"Lebed was the guarantor. If Chechnya flares up again I think it will be with a vengeance and the likelihood of a new settlement would seem more remote than ever," Gaddy said.
The United States has had mixed feelings about Lebed.

Officials welcomed his success in negotiating an end to fighting in Chechnya -- where the Russian army launched massive attacks on the civilian population -- and also praised comments he made during a visit to Brussels this month that appeared to take a flexible view of NATO expansion.
But U.S. officials also have seen him as a loose cannon and condemned comments he made that they said were hostile to religious groups including Jews and Roman Catholics.
